note.explanation: Temperature tells how hot or cold something is. Heat is energy transferred from a warmer object to a cooler one. Thermometers use a property that changes with temperature to measure temperature.
examples: Heat flows from a hot cup of tea to the cooler air around it.
A liquid-in-glass thermometer uses the change in the liquid’s volume as its thermometric property.
note.checkAnswer: Heat is energy in transit from a warmer object to a cooler object because of a temperature difference.
note.simple: Temperature tells how hot or cold a body is. Heat is energy moving from a hotter body to a colder body.
note.checkQuestion: In which direction does heat flow when two bodies at different temperatures are in contact?
note.title: Temperature, Heat and Thermometers
steps: Compare the temperatures of the bodies.
Heat flows from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.
It continues to flow until they reach the same temperature.
note.answer: Heat flows from the hotter body to the colder body.

options: Rotate and vibrate randomly at their own positions
Move in a straight line from hot to cold ends.
mcqs.stem: Q7.1. How do the molecules in a solid behave?
rationales: Incorrect: molecules in a solid do not move freely and randomly through the substance.
Correct: solid molecules vibrate about fixed mean positions.
Incorrect: this does not describe the usual motion of molecules in a solid.
Incorrect: molecules do not travel from the hot end to the cold end in straight lines.

mcqs.stem: Q7.2. What type of motion is of the molecules in a gas?
rationales: Incorrect: gas molecules do not all move along one straight line.
Correct: gas molecules move randomly in different directions.
Incorrect: vibration about fixed positions is characteristic of particles in solids.
Incorrect: rotation alone does not describe the motion of gas molecules.

options: the total amount of heat contained in it
the total number of molecules in it
mcqs.stem: Q7.3. Temperature of a substance is:
rationales: Incorrect: heat is energy in transit, not an amount contained in a body.
Incorrect: temperature is not the number of molecules.
Correct: temperature indicates the degree of hotness or coldness.
Incorrect: intermolecular distance alone is not the definition of temperature.

options: total kinetic energy of the molecules
rationales: Incorrect: this is not the definition of heat.
Incorrect: internal energy is energy stored within a body, while heat is energy in transit.
Incorrect: heat is not defined as work done by molecules.
Correct: heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference.

mcqs.stem: Q7.5. In Kelvin scale, the temperature corresponding to melting point of ice is:
rationales: Incorrect: zero kelvin is absolute zero.
Incorrect: 32 is the Fahrenheit melting point of ice.
Incorrect: −273 is approximately the Celsius value of absolute zero, not the melting point of ice in kelvin.
Correct: the melting point of ice is approximately 273 K.

mcqs.stem: Q7.6. The temperature which has the same value on Celsius and Fahrenheit scale is:
rationales: Correct: −40° is the same reading on both scales.
Incorrect: +40° does not have the same numerical value on the two scales.
Incorrect: +45° does not have the same numerical value on the two scales.
Incorrect: −45° is not the common reading of the scales.

mcqs.stem: Q7.7. Which one is a better choice for a liquid-in-glass thermometer?
rationales: Incorrect: colourlessness makes the liquid harder to see.
Incorrect: a thermometer liquid should transfer heat readily, not be a bad conductor.
Correct: linear expansion makes the scale reliable and evenly spaced.
Incorrect: wetting glass can make the liquid level difficult to read accurately.

mcqs.stem: Q7.8. One disadvantage of using alcohol in a liquid-in-glass thermometer:
rationales: Incorrect: large expansivity is an advantage because it increases sensitivity.
Incorrect: a low freezing point is an advantage for measuring low temperatures.
Correct: alcohol wets the glass tube, making the level less distinct.
Incorrect: linear expansion is an advantage, not a disadvantage.

mcqs.stem: Q7.9. Water is not used as a thermometric liquid mainly due to:
rationales: Incorrect: colourlessness is a disadvantage but is not the main reason.
Incorrect: water’s conductivity is not the main reason it is unsuitable.
Correct: water does not expand uniformly with temperature, so its expansion is non-linear.
Incorrect: its boiling point is a limitation, but non-linear expansion is the main reason.

options: gives a large change for a given temperature rise
can measure a large range of temperature
mcqs.stem: Q7.10. A thermometer has a narrow capillary tube so that it:
rationales: Incorrect: quick response depends mainly on the thermometer’s thermal properties and construction.
Incorrect: a narrow capillary does not by itself retain the maximum reading.
Correct: a small volume expansion produces a larger movement along a narrow capillary.
Incorrect: a narrow capillary does not increase the temperature range.

mcqs.stem: Q7.11. Which thermometer is most suitable for recording rapidly varying temperature?
rationales: Correct: a thermocouple responds quickly to changing temperature.
Incorrect: a mercury-in-glass laboratory thermometer responds more slowly than a thermocouple.
Incorrect: an alcohol-in-glass thermometer is not the most suitable for rapid temperature changes.
Incorrect: a clinical thermometer is designed for body temperature, not rapidly varying temperatures.

written.text: Q7.1. Why solids have a fixed volume and shape according to particle theory of matter?
written.finalAnswer: Solid particles are closely packed and held in fixed positions; they only vibrate about their mean positions.

rubric.why: The particle arrangement explains why a solid keeps its shape.
rubric.description: State that solid particles are closely packed and held in fixed positions.
rubric.how: Mention the close spacing and fixed positions.

rubric.why: The limited movement explains why the particles do not flow or change the solid’s shape and volume.
rubric.description: State that particles only vibrate about their mean positions.
rubric.how: Describe their restricted motion.

modelAnswer: The particles in a solid are closely packed and held in fixed positions.
They only vibrate about their mean positions, so the solid has a fixed shape and volume.

written.text: Q7.2. What are the reasons that gases have neither a fixed volume nor a fixed shape?
written.finalAnswer: Gas particles are far apart, have weak intermolecular forces and move freely in random directions, so they spread to fill their container.

rubric.why: Large separation lets gas particles spread out.
rubric.description: State that gas particles are far apart.
rubric.how: Describe the large spaces between particles.

rubric.why: Free random motion explains why a gas takes the container’s shape and volume.
rubric.description: Explain that particles move freely and spread through the container.
rubric.how: Link free movement to the absence of a fixed shape and volume.

modelAnswer: Gas particles are far apart and the intermolecular forces between them are weak.
They move freely in random directions and spread to fill their container, so gases have no fixed shape or volume.

written.text: Q7.3. Compare the spacing of molecules in the solid, liquid and gaseous state.
written.finalAnswer: Molecules are very closely spaced in solids, less closely spaced in liquids, and very far apart in gases.

rubric.why: The solid comparison must identify the smallest spacing.
rubric.description: Give the spacing of molecules in solids and liquids.
rubric.how: State that solid particles are closest and liquid particles are less closely spaced.

rubric.why: The gas comparison must identify the largest spacing.
rubric.description: State that gas molecules are very far apart.
rubric.how: Identify the large spacing in a gas.

modelAnswer: In a solid, molecules are very closely packed.
In a liquid, molecules are less closely packed than in a solid.
In a gas, molecules are very far apart.

written.text: Q7.4. What is the effect of raising the temperature of a liquid?
written.finalAnswer: Its molecules gain kinetic energy, move faster and usually spread farther apart, so the liquid expands.

rubric.why: Increased molecular motion is the direct effect of heating.
rubric.description: State that molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster.
rubric.how: Describe the increase in molecular motion.

rubric.why: The increased separation explains the usual expansion of a liquid.
rubric.description: State that the liquid usually expands.
rubric.how: Link the increased motion to expansion.

modelAnswer: When the temperature of a liquid is raised, its molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster.
They usually spread farther apart, so the liquid expands.

written.text: Q7.5. What is meant by temperature of a body?
written.finalAnswer: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.

rubric.why: This is the required meaning of temperature.
rubric.description: Define temperature as the degree of hotness or coldness.
rubric.how: Give the definition clearly.

modelAnswer: Temperature of a body is the degree of hotness or coldness of that body.

written.text: Q7.6. Define heat as ‘energy in transit’.
written.finalAnswer: Heat is energy transferred from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature because of a temperature difference.

rubric.why: Heat is energy being transferred, not energy stored as a substance in a body.
rubric.description: Define heat as energy in transit or transfer.
rubric.how: Use the idea of energy being transferred.

rubric.why: The temperature difference determines the direction of heat transfer.
rubric.description: State that heat transfers from higher to lower temperature.
rubric.how: Name the direction of transfer.

modelAnswer: Heat is energy in transit from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature because of a temperature difference.

written.text: Q7.7. What is meant by thermometric property of a substance? Enlist some thermometric properties.
written.finalAnswer: A thermometric property is a property that changes with temperature and can be used to measure it; examples include volume, length, pressure and electrical resistance.

rubric.why: The definition must connect a measurable property with temperature.
rubric.description: Define a thermometric property.
rubric.how: State that it changes with temperature and is used to measure temperature.

rubric.why: Examples show how a thermometer can use different changing properties.
rubric.description: List examples of thermometric properties.
rubric.how: Give at least two suitable examples.

modelAnswer: A thermometric property is a property of a substance that changes with temperature and can be used to measure temperature.
Examples include volume, length, pressure and electrical resistance.

written.text: Q7.8. State the main scales used for the measurement of temperature.
written.finalAnswer: The main temperature scales are Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin.

rubric.why: Celsius and Fahrenheit are two of the main scales.
rubric.description: Name Celsius and Fahrenheit.
rubric.how: Write both scale names.

rubric.why: Kelvin is the third main scale.
rubric.description: Name the Kelvin scale.
rubric.how: Include Kelvin.

modelAnswer: The main scales used for measuring temperature are Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin.

written.text: Q7.9. What is meant by sensitivity of a thermometer?
written.finalAnswer: Sensitivity is the change in the thermometer’s reading for a given change in temperature.

rubric.why: Sensitivity concerns how much the thermometer’s indication changes.
rubric.description: Refer to a change in the thermometer reading.
rubric.how: State that the reading changes.

rubric.why: The reading change must be related to a temperature change.
rubric.description: Relate the reading change to a given temperature change.
rubric.how: State what temperature change causes the reading change.

modelAnswer: The sensitivity of a thermometer is the change in its reading for a given change in temperature.

written.text: Q7.10. What do you mean by the linearity of a thermometer?
written.finalAnswer: A thermometer is linear when equal temperature changes produce equal changes in its thermometric property or scale reading.

rubric.why: Linearity concerns equal intervals of temperature.
rubric.description: Refer to equal changes in temperature.
rubric.how: State that the temperature intervals are equal.

rubric.why: Equal temperature intervals must produce equal thermometer indications.
rubric.description: Relate equal temperature changes to equal changes in the property or reading.
rubric.how: Explain the uniform response.

modelAnswer: A thermometer is linear if equal changes in temperature produce equal changes in its thermometric property or scale reading.

written.text: Q7.11. What makes the scale reading of a thermometer accurate?
written.finalAnswer: A thermometer gives an accurate scale reading when it is properly calibrated, has a uniform scale and is read correctly at eye level.

rubric.why: Calibration sets the scale against known temperatures.
rubric.description: Mention calibration using known fixed points.
rubric.how: State that the scale must be properly calibrated.

rubric.why: A uniform scale and correct viewing help avoid reading error.
rubric.description: Mention a uniform scale or reading at eye level to avoid parallax.
rubric.how: Give a suitable factor that improves reading accuracy.

modelAnswer: The thermometer should be properly calibrated using known fixed points and have a uniform scale.
Its reading should be taken at eye level to avoid parallax error.

written.text: Q7.12. What does determine the direction of heat flow?
written.finalAnswer: The temperature difference determines the direction of heat flow: heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.

rubric.why: The temperature difference determines the direction of transfer.
rubric.description: Identify the temperature difference as the determining factor.
rubric.how: State what determines the direction.

rubric.why: The direction must be stated correctly.
rubric.description: State that heat flows from higher to lower temperature.
rubric.how: Name the warmer-to-cooler direction.

modelAnswer: The temperature difference determines the direction of heat flow.
Heat flows from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature.

written.text: Q7.13. Distinguish between the heat and internal energy.
written.finalAnswer: Heat is energy in transit between bodies because of a temperature difference; internal energy is the energy stored in a body due to the microscopic kinetic and potential energies of its particles.

rubric.why: Heat must be distinguished as energy being transferred, not stored.
rubric.description: Define heat as energy in transit.
rubric.how: State that heat transfers because of a temperature difference.

rubric.why: Internal energy belongs to the body and includes microscopic particle energies.
rubric.description: Describe internal energy as energy within a body.
rubric.how: Mention stored particle kinetic and potential energy.

modelAnswer: Heat is energy in transit between bodies because of a temperature difference.
Internal energy is the energy stored in a body due to the microscopic kinetic and potential energies of its particles.

written.text: Q7.14. When you touch a cold surface, does cold travel from the surface to your hand or does energy travel from your hand to cold surface?
written.finalAnswer: Energy travels from your warmer hand to the colder surface; cold does not travel.

rubric.why: The response must identify energy, rather than cold, as what transfers.
rubric.description: State that energy travels from the hand to the surface.
rubric.how: Identify the direction of energy transfer.

rubric.why: Heat transfer is from higher temperature to lower temperature.
rubric.description: Explain that cold itself does not travel.
rubric.how: State that the hand loses energy to the colder surface.

modelAnswer: Energy travels from your warmer hand to the colder surface.
Cold does not travel; heat energy transfers from higher temperature to lower temperature.

written.text: Q7.15. Can you feel your fever by touching your own forehead? Explain.
written.finalAnswer: No. Your hand and forehead are nearly at the same temperature, so little heat flows between them; a thermometer is needed to measure fever.

rubric.why: Touch cannot reliably detect fever when the hand and forehead are at similar temperatures.
rubric.description: Answer no and compare the temperatures.
rubric.how: Explain that the hand and forehead are nearly at the same temperature.

rubric.why: A thermometer is needed for an objective temperature measurement.
rubric.description: State why touch is insufficient and/or identify a thermometer as the measuring instrument.
rubric.how: Mention the small heat flow or the need for a thermometer.

modelAnswer: No. Your hand and forehead are nearly at the same temperature, so little heat flows between them.
A thermometer is needed to measure whether you have a fever.

written.text: Q7.1. Is kinetic molecular theory of matter applicable to the plasma state of matter? Describe briefly.
written.finalAnswer: Yes. Plasma consists of ionised particles which are in continuous random motion; their motion and interactions can be described by kinetic molecular theory.

rubric.why: The answer must directly address whether the theory applies.
rubric.description: State that the theory is applicable.
rubric.how: Give a clear yes.

rubric.why: Plasma consists of charged, ionised particles.
rubric.description: Identify the particles in plasma.
rubric.how: Mention ions or ionised particles and electrons.

rubric.why: Particle motion is central to the kinetic molecular theory.
rubric.description: Describe the motion of plasma particles.
rubric.how: State that the particles are in continuous motion.

rubric.why: The explanation must link plasma particles to the theory’s description of matter.
rubric.description: Connect particle motion and interactions with the theory.
rubric.how: Explain briefly why the theory applies.

modelAnswer: Yes, kinetic molecular theory is applicable to plasma.
Plasma consists of ionised particles, including ions and electrons.
These particles are in continuous random motion.
Their motion and interactions can be described by kinetic molecular theory.

written.text: Q7.2. Why is mercury usually preferred to alcohol as a thermometric liquid?
written.finalAnswer: Mercury expands nearly linearly, does not wet glass, is easy to see and conducts heat well; it also has a higher boiling point than alcohol.

rubric.why: Uniform expansion supports a dependable scale.
rubric.description: Give the advantage of nearly linear expansion.
rubric.how: State that mercury expands uniformly or nearly linearly.

rubric.why: A distinct mercury level is easier to read.
rubric.description: State that mercury does not wet glass.
rubric.how: Link this property to a clear level.

rubric.why: Visibility or good thermal conductivity is a useful thermometer property.
rubric.description: Give another advantage such as visibility or good conductivity.
rubric.how: Name a relevant practical property.

rubric.why: Mercury can measure higher temperatures than alcohol before boiling.
rubric.description: State its comparatively high boiling point.
rubric.how: Compare its upper-use temperature with alcohol.

modelAnswer: Mercury expands nearly linearly with temperature and does not wet glass, so its level is clear and the scale is uniform.
It is easy to see and conducts heat well.
It also has a higher boiling point than alcohol, so it can measure higher temperatures.

written.text: Q7.3. Why is water not suitable for use in thermometers? Without calculations, guess what is equivalent temperature of 373 K on Celsius and Fahrenheit scales?
written.finalAnswer: Water is unsuitable because its expansion is non-linear. 373 K is about 100°C and 212°F.

rubric.why: Non-uniform expansion makes water unsuitable for a thermometer scale.
rubric.description: Give the main reason water is unsuitable.
rubric.how: State that its expansion is non-linear.

rubric.why: This is the approximate Celsius equivalent of 373 K.
rubric.description: Give the Celsius equivalent.
rubric.how: Write approximately 100°C.

rubric.why: This is the approximate Fahrenheit equivalent of 100°C.
rubric.description: Give the Fahrenheit equivalent.
rubric.how: Write approximately 212°F.

rubric.why: Recognising 373 K as close to the boiling point of water supports the estimate.
rubric.description: Show the temperature-scale reasoning or identify it as approximately the boiling point of water.
rubric.how: Connect 373 K with 100°C.

modelAnswer: Water is not suitable because it expands non-linearly with temperature.
373 K is approximately 100°C.
The equivalent temperature is approximately 212°F.

written.text: Q7.4. Mention two ways in which the design of a liquid-in-glass thermometer may be altered to increase its sensitivity.
written.finalAnswer: Use a narrower capillary tube and a larger bulb containing more thermometric liquid.

rubric.why: A narrow tube makes a small volume expansion produce a greater length change.
rubric.description: Give the narrower-capillary design change and its effect.
rubric.how: State that a narrower capillary increases the movement for a given temperature change.

rubric.why: More liquid expanding produces a greater movement in the tube.
rubric.description: Give the larger-bulb or greater-liquid-volume change and its effect.
rubric.how: State that more thermometric liquid increases the movement.

modelAnswer: Use a narrower capillary tube so a small expansion makes the liquid level rise farther.
Use a larger bulb containing more thermometric liquid so its expansion produces a greater change in the capillary level.

written.text: Q7.5. One litre of water is heated by a stove and its temperature rises by 2°C. If two litres of water is heated on the same stove for the same time, what will be then rise in temperature?

rubric.why: The same stove heating for the same time supplies approximately the same heat energy.
rubric.description: Recognise that the heat supplied is unchanged.
rubric.how: State that heating conditions are the same.

rubric.why: Twice the water mass requires twice as much energy for the same temperature rise.
rubric.description: Recognise that the water quantity is doubled.
rubric.how: Compare two litres with one litre.

rubric.why: With twice the water and the same heat, the temperature rise is halved.
rubric.description: Find the new temperature rise.
rubric.how: Halve 2°C.

rubric.why: The correct numerical response is 1°C.
rubric.description: Give the final temperature rise with its unit.
rubric.how: Write 1°C.

modelAnswer: The same stove for the same time supplies the same heat energy.
Two litres is twice the amount of water, so the temperature rise is half as much.
Temperature rise = 2°C ÷ 2 = 1°C.

written.text: Q7.6. Why are there no negative numbers on the Kelvin scale?
written.finalAnswer: The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, so temperatures below 0 K are not possible.

rubric.why: Absolute zero is the zero point of the Kelvin scale.
rubric.description: Identify the Kelvin zero as absolute zero.
rubric.how: State that 0 K represents absolute zero.

rubric.why: There are no temperatures below absolute zero in the scale used here.
rubric.description: Explain why negative Kelvin values do not occur.
rubric.how: State that no temperature is below 0 K.

modelAnswer: The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, which is 0 K.
Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature, so temperatures below 0 K are not possible.

written.text: Q7.7. Comment on the statement. "A thermometer measures its own temperature."
written.finalAnswer: The statement is correct: a thermometer reaches thermal equilibrium with the body, and its own temperature then indicates the body’s temperature.

rubric.why: A thermometer directly has the temperature it senses.
rubric.description: Assess the statement.
rubric.how: Say that the statement is correct.

rubric.why: Thermal equilibrium lets the thermometer and body share a temperature.
rubric.description: Explain that the thermometer comes to the same temperature as the body.
rubric.how: Mention thermal equilibrium.

rubric.why: The thermometer’s temperature is used to infer the body’s temperature.
rubric.description: Link the thermometer reading to the body temperature.
rubric.how: State what the thermometer’s temperature indicates.

modelAnswer: The statement is correct: a thermometer measures its own temperature.
When placed in contact with a body, it reaches thermal equilibrium with the body.
At equilibrium, the thermometer and body have the same temperature, so its reading indicates the body’s temperature.

written.text: Q7.8. There are various objects made of cotton, wood, plastic, metals, etc. In a winter night, compare their temperatures with the air temperature by touching them with your hand.
written.finalAnswer: After being in the room long enough, the objects and air are approximately at the same temperature. Metal feels colder because it conducts heat away from the hand faster, not necessarily because its temperature is lower.

rubric.why: Objects left in the same surroundings reach approximately thermal equilibrium with the air.
rubric.description: Compare the actual temperatures of the objects and air.
rubric.how: State that they are approximately equal after sufficient time.

rubric.why: Touch sensation depends on the rate of heat transfer, not only the actual temperature.
rubric.description: Explain why metal feels colder than cotton, wood or plastic.
rubric.how: Mention metal’s greater thermal conductivity and faster heat transfer from the hand.

modelAnswer: If the objects have been in the room long enough, they are approximately at the same temperature as the air.
Metal may feel colder because it conducts heat away from the hand faster than cotton, wood or plastic.
The sensation does not necessarily mean that the metal is at a lower temperature.

written.text: Q7.9. Which is greater; an increase in temperature 1°C or one 1°F?
written.finalAnswer: An increase of 1°C is greater; it equals an increase of 1.8°F.

rubric.why: A one-degree Celsius interval is larger than a one-degree Fahrenheit interval.
rubric.description: Identify which increase is greater.
rubric.how: Choose 1°C.

rubric.why: This states the interval conversion and supports the comparison.
rubric.description: Give the equivalent Fahrenheit interval.
rubric.how: State that 1°C equals 1.8°F.

modelAnswer: An increase of 1°C is greater than an increase of 1°F.
An increase of 1°C equals an increase of 1.8°F.

written.text: Q7.10. Why would not you expect all the molecules in a gas to have the same speed?
written.finalAnswer: Gas molecules collide and exchange energy, so they have a range of kinetic energies and speeds at any instant.

rubric.why: Collisions change the motions of gas molecules.
rubric.description: Mention collisions between gas molecules.
rubric.how: State that molecules collide.

rubric.why: Energy exchange means molecules do not all have the same speed.
rubric.description: Explain that molecules have differing speeds and kinetic energies.
rubric.how: Link collisions or energy exchange to a range of speeds.

modelAnswer: Gas molecules collide with one another and exchange energy.
Therefore, at any instant they have a range of kinetic energies and do not all have the same speed.

written.text: Q7.11. Does it make sense to talk about the temperature of a vacuum?
written.finalAnswer: In an ideal vacuum there are no particles, so the usual particle-based meaning of temperature does not apply directly; radiation in the vacuum can still have a temperature.

rubric.why: The usual temperature description concerns the motion and energy of particles.
rubric.description: Explain the difficulty of assigning ordinary temperature to an ideal vacuum.
rubric.how: State that an ideal vacuum has no particles.

rubric.why: A careful answer distinguishes a vacuum from radiation present in it.
rubric.description: Qualify the answer by noting that radiation can have a temperature.
rubric.how: Mention radiation or clarify the limit of the ordinary particle-based definition.

modelAnswer: An ideal vacuum contains no particles, so the usual particle-based meaning of temperature does not apply directly to it.
However, radiation present in a vacuum can have a temperature.

written.text: Q7.12. Comment on the statement: “A hot body does not contain heat”.
written.finalAnswer: The statement is correct in physics: a body contains internal energy, while heat is energy transferred between bodies because of a temperature difference.

rubric.why: The statement distinguishes stored energy from energy in transfer.
rubric.description: Assess the statement as correct in the physics sense.
rubric.how: State that the body does not contain heat.

rubric.why: A body’s energy is described as internal energy, not heat.
rubric.description: State what energy a hot body contains.
rubric.how: Name internal energy.

rubric.why: Heat is defined as energy transfer due to a temperature difference.
rubric.description: Define heat correctly.
rubric.how: State that heat is energy in transit.

modelAnswer: The statement is correct in physics: a hot body does not contain heat.
It contains internal energy.
Heat is energy in transit from one body to another because of a temperature difference.

written.text: Q7.13. Discuss whether the Sun is matter.
written.finalAnswer: Yes. The Sun is matter because it has mass and occupies space; it is mostly hot plasma.

rubric.why: The response must give a clear decision.
rubric.description: State that the Sun is matter.
rubric.how: Answer yes.

rubric.why: Having mass and occupying space are properties of matter.
rubric.description: Give the reasons the Sun is matter.
rubric.how: Mention mass and that it occupies space.

rubric.why: The Sun’s main state of matter is plasma.
rubric.description: Identify the Sun’s material state.
rubric.how: Mention plasma.

modelAnswer: Yes, the Sun is matter because it has mass and occupies space.
The Sun is mostly hot plasma.

written.text: Q7.1. Describe the main points of particle theory of matter which differentiate solids, liquids and gases.
written.finalAnswer: Matter consists of particles. In solids, particles are closely packed and vibrate about fixed mean positions; in liquids, they are close together but can move past one another; in gases, they are far apart and move freely and randomly. Their spacing, motion and intermolecular forces account for the different shapes and volumes.

rubric.why: The answer should begin with the particle model common to all states.
rubric.description: State that matter consists of particles.
rubric.how: Introduce the particle theory.

rubric.why: Solid particle spacing and restricted motion explain its fixed shape and volume.
rubric.description: Describe solid particles.
rubric.how: Mention close packing and vibration about fixed positions.

rubric.why: Liquid particles can move relative to one another while remaining close.
rubric.description: Describe liquid particles.
rubric.how: Mention close spacing and movement past each other.

rubric.why: Gas spacing and movement explain why it fills its container.
rubric.description: Describe gas particles.
rubric.how: Mention large spacing and free random motion.

rubric.why: The comparison should connect particle properties to the states’ macroscopic behaviour.
rubric.description: Link particle differences to shape, volume or intermolecular forces.
rubric.how: Explain how particle arrangement and motion distinguish the states.

modelAnswer: Matter consists of tiny particles.
In a solid, particles are very closely packed, strongly attracted and vibrate about fixed mean positions; a solid has fixed shape and volume.
In a liquid, particles are close together but can move past one another; a liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.
In a gas, particles are far apart, weakly attracted and move freely in random directions; a gas has neither fixed shape nor fixed volume.
Thus, particle spacing, motion and intermolecular forces differentiate solids, liquids and gases.

written.text: Q7.2. What is temperature? How is it measured? Describe briefly the construction of a mercury-in-glass thermometer.
written.finalAnswer: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body. It is measured with a thermometer using a thermometric property. A mercury-in-glass thermometer has a mercury-filled bulb connected to a narrow graduated capillary tube, sealed at the top; the mercury level indicates temperature.

rubric.why: The response must define temperature.
rubric.description: Define temperature.
rubric.how: State that it is the degree of hotness or coldness.

rubric.why: The answer must explain the measurement method.
rubric.description: State that a thermometer measures temperature using a changing property.
rubric.how: Mention a thermometer and thermometric property.

rubric.why: The bulb contains the thermometric liquid.
rubric.description: Describe the mercury-filled bulb.
rubric.how: Identify the bulb and mercury.

rubric.why: The capillary and scale make the liquid expansion readable.

modelAnswer: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
It is measured by a thermometer using a thermometric property that changes with temperature.
A mercury-in-glass thermometer has a bulb containing mercury, connected to a narrow capillary tube.
The tube is graduated and sealed at the top.
As temperature changes, the mercury level moves along the scale and indicates the temperature.

written.text: Q7.3. Compare the three scales used for measuring temperature.
written.finalAnswer: The Celsius scale has ice and steam points 0°C and 100°C; the Fahrenheit scale has 32°F and 212°F; the Kelvin scale has 273 K and 373 K. Each interval is divided into 100 Celsius, 180 Fahrenheit or 100 kelvin divisions. Kelvin starts at absolute zero and has no degree symbol.

rubric.why: The Celsius fixed points are needed for comparison.
rubric.description: Give Celsius fixed points.
rubric.how: State 0°C and 100°C for ice and steam points.

rubric.why: The Fahrenheit scale has different numerical fixed points.
rubric.description: Give Fahrenheit fixed points.
rubric.how: State 32°F and 212°F.

rubric.why: The Kelvin fixed points provide the absolute scale values.
rubric.description: Give Kelvin fixed points.
rubric.how: State approximately 273 K and 373 K.

rubric.why: Comparing interval sizes distinguishes Fahrenheit from Celsius and Kelvin.
rubric.description: Compare the scale divisions.
rubric.how: State 100, 180 and 100 divisions respectively.

rubric.why: The Kelvin scale is an absolute scale and uses K without a degree sign.
rubric.description: State a distinguishing feature of Kelvin.
rubric.how: Mention absolute zero or its notation.

modelAnswer: On the Celsius scale, the ice point is 0°C and the steam point is 100°C.
On the Fahrenheit scale, the ice point is 32°F and the steam point is 212°F.
On the Kelvin scale, these points are approximately 273 K and 373 K.
The interval between the fixed points has 100 Celsius divisions, 180 Fahrenheit divisions and 100 kelvin divisions.
Kelvin starts at absolute zero and its unit is written K, without a degree symbol.

written.text: Q7.4. What is meant by sensitive, range and linearity of thermometers? Explain with examples.
written.finalAnswer: Sensitivity is the change in reading for a given temperature change; range is the interval of temperatures a thermometer can measure; linearity means equal temperature changes produce equal scale changes. A narrow capillary increases sensitivity, a clinical thermometer has a limited range, and a linear scale has equal intervals.

rubric.why: Sensitivity describes how much the reading responds to temperature.
rubric.description: Define sensitivity.
rubric.how: Relate reading change to temperature change.

rubric.why: Range states the temperatures over which the instrument works.
rubric.description: Define range.
rubric.how: State the lowest-to-highest measurable interval.

rubric.why: Linearity describes uniform response over the scale.
rubric.description: Define linearity.
rubric.how: Explain equal temperature changes give equal scale changes.

rubric.why: An appropriate example demonstrates sensitivity or range.
rubric.description: Give a suitable example for one property.
rubric.how: Use a narrow capillary or clinical thermometer example.

rubric.why: An example makes the meaning of linearity or another property clear.
rubric.description: Give an example illustrating uniform scale divisions.
rubric.how: Explain that equal scale intervals represent equal temperature intervals.

modelAnswer: Sensitivity is the change in a thermometer’s reading for a given change in temperature; a narrow capillary makes a thermometer more sensitive.
Range is the interval of temperatures that a thermometer can measure; a clinical thermometer has a limited range suitable for body temperature.
Linearity means equal changes in temperature produce equal changes in the thermometric property and scale reading.
For example, on a linear scale, equal lengths represent equal temperature intervals.

written.text: Q7.5. Explain, how the parameters mentioned in question 7.4 are improved in the structure of liquid-in-glass thermometer.
written.finalAnswer: Sensitivity is increased by a narrow capillary and a large bulb; range is increased by a suitable thermometric liquid and sufficient capillary length; linearity is improved by using a liquid that expands uniformly with temperature and a uniform capillary.

rubric.why: The bulb and capillary determine how far the liquid moves for a temperature change.
rubric.description: Explain how sensitivity is improved.
rubric.how: Mention a narrow capillary and/or a large bulb, with their effect.

rubric.why: Range depends on the liquid’s usable temperature limits and tube capacity.
rubric.description: Explain what design choices affect range.
rubric.how: Mention an appropriate liquid and adequate capillary length.

rubric.why: Uniform expansion supports an evenly spaced scale.
rubric.description: Explain how linearity is improved.
rubric.how: Select a liquid with uniform expansion.

rubric.why: The scale structure must provide equal readings for equal temperature intervals.
rubric.description: Mention the scale or capillary feature supporting linearity.
rubric.how: State that a uniform scale or tube gives equal intervals.

modelAnswer: Sensitivity is increased by using a large bulb and a narrow capillary tube, so expansion gives a large rise of the liquid level.
The range depends on the thermometric liquid’s working temperature limits and on providing sufficient capillary length.
Linearity is improved by choosing a liquid that expands uniformly with temperature.
A uniform capillary and scale give equal scale intervals for equal temperature intervals.

written.text: Q7.6. The length between the fixed point of liquid-in-glass thermometer is 20 cm. If the mercury level is 4.5 cm above the lower mark, what is the temperature on the Fahrenheit scale?

rubric.why: The measured rise must be compared with the full fixed-point interval.
rubric.description: Set up the Fahrenheit scale proportion.
rubric.how: Relate 4.5 cm out of 20 cm to the 180°F interval above 32°F.

rubric.why: The rise above the lower fixed point is 40.5 Fahrenheit degrees.
rubric.description: Calculate the rise above 32°F.
rubric.how: Evaluate 180 × 4.5/20.

rubric.why: The scale begins at 32°F, so the rise must be added to 32°F.
rubric.description: Find the Fahrenheit reading.
rubric.how: Add the calculated rise to 32°F.

rubric.why: The final answer must include the correct unit.
rubric.description: Give the final temperature.
rubric.how: Write 72.5°F.

modelAnswer: The interval between the fixed points corresponds to 212°F − 32°F = 180°F.
Rise above the lower point = (4.5/20) × 180°F = 40.5°F
Temperature = 32°F + 40.5°F = 72.5°F
Answer: 72.5°F

examTips: Section A asks direct concept and property MCQs; learn the particle motions, scale fixed points and thermometer advantages and disadvantages.
Short questions usually earn marks for a clear definition or distinction plus a brief reason or example.
Constructed-response and comprehensive questions are marked for relevant points in sequence; use terms such as thermal equilibrium, thermometric property, linear expansion and absolute zero.
For thermometer-design questions, link each design feature to its effect, such as a narrow capillary giving a larger movement and greater sensitivity.
For numerical problems, write the scale relation or proportion, substitute values, show working and include the unit with the final answer.
Use Kelvin as K, not °K, and remember that Kelvin temperature is approximately Celsius temperature plus 273.

explain.title: Particles in the three states
explain.body: Matter is made of particles. In a solid, particles are closely packed and vibrate about mean positions. In a liquid, particles remain close but can move past one another. In a gas, particles are far apart and move freely in random directions.

explain.title: Temperature and heat
explain.body: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body. Heat is energy in transit from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature. A body contains internal energy, not heat.

explain.title: Thermometers and their properties
explain.body: A thermometer uses a thermometric property that changes with temperature. Sensitivity describes the change in reading for a temperature change; range is the interval it can measure; linearity means equal temperature changes give equal scale changes.

explain.title: Temperature scales
explain.body: The Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales use different fixed-point readings. For ice and steam points they are 0°C and 100°C, 32°F and 212°F, and approximately 273 K and 373 K. Kelvin starts at absolute zero.

explain.title: Liquid-in-glass thermometers
explain.body: A liquid-in-glass thermometer has a bulb and a narrow graduated capillary. A large bulb and narrow capillary improve sensitivity. A liquid that expands uniformly gives a more linear scale; the liquid’s properties and tube length affect the range.

mistakes: Do not say that a body contains heat; it contains internal energy, while heat is energy in transit.
Do not confuse temperature with the total amount of heat or the number of molecules in a body.
When comparing thermometers, distinguish sensitivity, range and linearity and connect a design feature to the relevant property.
In temperature conversions, do not forget the +32 or −32 in Fahrenheit–Celsius conversions.
For a liquid-in-glass fixed-point problem, use the fraction of the full interval and include the lower point where required.
Write kelvin as K, not °K, and include units in numerical answers.
